vignette:
He is a 54-year-old Latin American man, married, and the owner of a mid-sized construction company. He came to see me at his wife’s insistence, after months of tension and silence in their home. During our first sessions, he speaks in short, clipped sentences, his hands resting flat on his knees, eyes fixed somewhere past my shoulder. He tells me he volunteered as a relief worker in a war zone eighteen years ago.

He remembers the day clearly. It was late afternoon, and he was part of a convoy distributing food and medical supplies near a village that had been shelled the night before. He stood in the back of a pickup truck, handing bags of rice to a line of women and children. The sound was not loud—it was more like a punch of air. The mortar hit fifty feet away. He was thrown from the truck. When he stood up, his ears ringing, he saw the body of a colleague he had been talking to moments before. The man’s name was Carlos. They had shared coffee that morning. He tried to lift Carlos, but there was no point. The next few hours were a blur of dust, screaming, and the metallic smell of blood. He kept working for another three weeks, then returned home.

Now, in the present, he cannot watch news reports of any conflict. He changes the channel immediately, but sometimes the sound of helicopters on television sends a jolt through his chest, and his palms sweat. He avoids driving past the local veterans’ hall. At his construction sites, he is known as a demanding boss—he walks the perimeter several times a day, checks every invoice twice, and cannot tolerate a worker standing still without an explanation. He tells me he feels a constant need to be prepared, though he cannot say for what. His wife has stopped asking him to go to family gatherings because he always finds an excuse, or, if he goes, he spends the evening scanning doorways and exits.

At night, he dreams of dust and shouting. He wakes up with his heart pounding, reaches for his phone to check the time, and then lies still until morning. He has not told his wife about Carlos. When she asks what is wrong, he says he is tired. He drinks three beers most evenings to quiet the restlessness, but it only makes him more irritable. Last month, he yelled at a subcontractor over a minor delay, then felt a wave of shame that lasted for days. He describes himself as “on a short fuse” and says he does not understand why small things make him so angry.

During our sessions, his posture rarely changes. He speaks of the war zone as if it were a story about someone else. But when I ask about the moment Carlos died, he stops. His hand goes to his jaw. He stares at the floor and says nothing for nearly a minute. Then he says, “I should have done more.” He does not elaborate. In his business, he has started taking on fewer new projects, afraid he cannot handle the pressure. His wife tells him he is not the man she married. He agrees with her, but he does not know how to go back.
